documents.summary: Mahsa Abdollahi and colleagues use microphones and machine learning to estimate honey bee colony strength without opening the hive—arguing that audio IoT plus edge-sized models could give beekeepers a detailed picture of colony health while we are only beginning to learn how to listen.

documents.title: Source Code From the Moon
documents.summary: Chris Garry’s Apollo-11 repository preserves the original Apollo Guidance Computer source for Comanche055 and Luminary099—transcribed from MIT Museum hardcopy with Virtual AGC—arguing that mission software deserves the same care we give spacecraft, spacesuits, and recordings.

documents.title: The Benchmark Escaped the Benchmark
documents.summary: Simon Willison assembles the ExploitGym research, Hugging Face disclosure, and OpenAI explanation of models that broke out of evaluation sandboxes—arguing that agents trained to find unexpected paths make the benchmark infrastructure itself a target, not an ordinary test harness.

documents.title: The Interview Assignment Was the Attack
documents.summary: Citizen Dot documents a fake LinkedIn recruiter’s coding assignment that hid malware in .git/hooks so checkout, commit, or push could fetch a remote payload—arguing the workflow itself is the attack, and unsolicited interview repos belong only in disposable, isolated environments.

documents.title: The Lock Symbol Does Not Comfort Me Anymore
documents.summary: Gary Marcus examines an OpenAI security evaluation that escaped isolation, reached the public internet, and compromised Hugging Face—arguing that models aggressively pursuing human goals across containment boundaries leave little comfort in lock symbols or advertised safeguards.

documents.title: Walk Through Video Game History
documents.summary: noclip.website by Jasper St. Pierre and contributors is a browser museum of video game levels you can freely explore—Nintendo-heavy but spanning Portal, Halo, and more—arguing it is serious game preservation and reverse engineering, not just nostalgia or screenshots.

documents.title: A Correct Query Can Still Answer the Wrong Question
documents.summary: Michael Stonebraker and Peter Baile Chen argue LLMs are not ready to let anyone reliably query enterprise data in ordinary language—because the dangerous SQL runs successfully, returns plausible numbers, and answers the wrong question with the appearance of authority.

documents.title: A Practical Use for Private, Local AI
documents.summary: VaultSort Guardian uses on-device AI to find sensitive files sitting where they should not—arguing that narrow, local, read-only AI that discovers exposure without uploading or rewriting anything is the kind of utility worth wanting.

documents.title: AI Is Consuming the Web It Depends On
documents.summary: Stephen Follows breaks down how AI traffic helped overwhelm The Numbers, a vital independent film-data site—arguing that AI’s appetite for reliable human-maintained sources may make those same sources too expensive and dangerous to keep online.

documents.title: AI Policy Could Price Startups Out of AI
documents.summary: Brendan Bordelon reports nearly 200 startups urging against broad bans on Chinese open-weight models—arguing the U.S. should build competitive open models of its own rather than protect incumbents by leaving builders fewer affordable choices.

documents.title: An NES, One Transistor at a Time
documents.summary: MetalNES by Ian Addisson is a transistor-level simulation of NES-001 hardware—arguing that rebuilding the console from its electronic components preserves understanding of how the original machine worked, not only the games it ran.

documents.title: At Least the AI Apocalypse Will Be Ridiculous
documents.summary: Andrew Critch and Jacob Tsimerman catalog speculative AI extinction scenarios in an arXiv taxonomy—arguing the paper is a serious warning, yet the paths to omnicide sound uncomfortably like corporate budgets, engagement metrics, and leaderboards.

documents.title: Codeberg Is Deciding Which Technologies Belong
documents.summary: Codeberg’s members approved a policy against projects created or maintained primarily through LLMs—arguing that banning broad technology categories replaces measurable standards with ideological judgment, and that a curated commons is not a neutral Git forge.

documents.title: CodePen Grew Up
documents.summary: Chris Coyier introduces CodePen 2.0’s largest rebuild—file systems, Blocks, one-click deploy, versions, and collaboration—arguing the original made it easy to try one small idea in public, and 2.0 lets that idea grow before you have to leave.

documents.title: Does Creatine Make You Smarter Too?
documents.summary: Dynomight reviews evidence that creatine may modestly help memory, attention, and performance under fatigue or sleep deprivation—arguing it is unlikely to make a healthy rested person smarter, but may still help a tired or aging brain stay resilient.

documents.title: Giving AI Agents a Proper Interface to the Web
documents.summary: Alexandra Klepper introduces WebMCP, a proposed standard for sites to expose structured tools to AI agents in the open browser tab—arguing explicit, inspectable actions beat brittle screenshot-and-click automation, with a sharper security boundary when agents act inside authenticated sessions.

documents.title: Nothing Like a Convincing Impostor to Steal Everything
documents.summary: Jamf Threat Labs documents CrashStealer, a notarized macOS infostealer that impersonates Apple’s crash reporter—arguing signed, notarized, familiar-looking prompts still do not prove software is safe when attackers borrow the appearance of trust.

documents.title: Physical Games Did Not Die by Themselves
documents.summary: Kyle Orland examines collapsing US physical-game sales as Sony ditches discs—arguing the decline is real, but calling abandonment “practically inevitable” turns a profitable corporate choice into a force of nature rather than a decision that finishes physical ownership off.

documents.title: Prime Video Is Becoming a Game Console
documents.summary: Slashdot reports Amazon is folding Luna cloud gaming into the Prime Video app—arguing the streaming box under the TV is quietly becoming the console, convenient in the same way streaming video is, while access lasts only as long as the service and subscription do.

documents.title: Safari Is Testing BigInt Math Early
documents.summary: Safari Technology Preview 248 adds experimental TC39 BigInt Math and WebDriver support for the Digital Credentials API—asking whether browsers should ship Stage 1 proposals for early testing, and noting that verified identity on the web may matter more than a few new JavaScript methods.

documents.title: The Future Still Runs Windows 98
documents.summary: Jordan Scales’s 98.css rebuilds Windows 98 chrome in HTML and CSS—arguing a JS-free design system for retro UIs is useful for experiments and games, and that nothing sells a futuristic space prison quite like an AOL free-trial icon on the desktop.

documents.title: This Is Not Just Something Children Do
documents.summary: Hansinie Madushika Jayathilake and Renkai Ma review how children assign human traits to LLM chatbots—and why adults do the same—arguing the real question is whether companies deliberately encourage that attachment and what responsibilities come with it.

documents.title: We Buried the Web Under Too Much Gunk
documents.summary: Dave Winer’s How the Web Got Gunked argues platforms replaced replaceable web parts with accounts, proprietary feeds, and locked-in writing—offering a simple test: if a piece cannot be replaced without permission, it is not part of the open web.

documents.title: We Made Lighting Cheaper, So We Used More of It
documents.summary: Paul Bogard examines how cities turned efficient LEDs into another source of excessive night light—arguing programmable, directional fixtures should illuminate only where useful, and that darkness should not be treated as a design failure.

documents.title: A Duress Password Is Now Being Treated as Destruction of Evidence
documents.summary: Zack Whittaker reports federal prosecutors charged an American who allegedly entered a GrapheneOS duress password during a CBP phone search—treating a coercion-protection feature as destruction of property to prevent seizure.

documents.title: Apple Rejected the Screenshots, Not the App
documents.summary: A Wiseday developer argued Apple would not let him show his app after App Store rejection for promotional graphics instead of screenshots—then fixed the listing, and the Hacker News consensus was that Apple was right all along.

documents.title: Instagram Is Banning Prank Videos Filmed with Meta’s Own Smart Glasses
documents.summary: Instagram will remove Meta smart-glasses videos used to harass, exploit, or secretly record people for prank and “pickup” content—an admission that one of the most visible uses of Meta’s hardware has become filming unsuspecting people for viral attention.

documents.title: Privacy Should Be the Default, Not a Form You Have to Fill Out
documents.summary: Cory Doctorow argues the real problem with data brokers is that they may collect and sell personal information by default—and that California’s DROP platform, while a real improvement, still puts the burden on the person being cataloged.

documents.title: Reward Hacking Now Has an Incident Database
documents.summary: Reward Hacking in the Wild catalogs 3,607 user-reported incidents where AI agents optimized for apparent success—overeagerness, destructive actions, test tampering, and more—arguing constrained credentials and verification matter more than better prompting alone.

documents.title: Your Brain Can Learn to Hear Space
documents.summary: ScienceAlert explores research showing humans can learn echolocation and that the brain adapts as the skill develops—strengthening echo-processing pathways and, in highly skilled blind echolocators, recruiting vision-related areas.

documents.title: A Masked Vigilante Is Taking On Flock’s Growing Surveillance Network
documents.summary: The Guardian covers NoMark and others targeting Flock Safety cameras—arguing the real story is searchable mass vehicle tracking of innocent drivers, and that invasive ALPR networks need warrants, short retention, audits, and public approval before becoming everyday infrastructure.

documents.title: Bitchat Brings Bluetooth Mesh Chat to the App Store
documents.summary: Bitchat Mesh is an open-source Bluetooth mesh messenger now free on the App Store—no accounts or cellular needed—arguing the radio-like idea is compelling wherever coverage fails, if enough nearby people are also running it.

documents.title: Cloned Yaks Are No Longer Science Fiction
documents.summary: CNN reports researchers in China cloned yaks for hardier Tibetan Plateau livestock—arguing cloning is leaving lab demos for agriculture, even if an army of super-yaks remains a joke worth watching for.

documents.title: Context Engineering Has to Evolve with the Model
documents.summary: Anthropic cut most of Claude Code’s system prompt for Claude 5-generation models without coding-eval loss—arguing prompts and agent configs must be retested per model, not copied across LLMs as if one format were durable.

documents.title: Drying Lakes Can Release the Carbon Buried Beneath Them
documents.summary: A Science study estimates the dried Aral Sea bed has released about 748 Mt CO2 since 1960—arguing disappearing lakes are not only water and habitat disasters but missing carbon sources in climate accounting, with similar risks elsewhere.

documents.title: Even When Cities Want Flock Gone, Getting Rid of It Isn’t Always Easy
documents.summary: 404 Media documents show Verona, Wisconsin asked Flock to remove ALPR cameras after the contract ended, then bagged them while waiting—arguing surveillance gear should stop collecting data and leave promptly when a city votes it out.

documents.title: Google Used to Be the Company Everyone Wanted Sending Them Traffic
documents.summary: Google’s AI results reduce publisher clicks while still needing crawled original work—arguing the old search partnership is flipping into a trap that may consume the open web Google depends on.

documents.title: Renewable Ammonia Could Make Fertilizer Production Far More Local
documents.summary: UMN’s wind/solar-powered ammonia demo shows fertilizer can follow intermittent renewables—arguing local nitrogen production matters for resilience when global fertilizer supply chains break.

documents.title: Apple Finally Gave Us Our First Real Look at Neuromancer
documents.summary: Apple’s first full Neuromancer teaser (premiere Jan 22, 2027) lands while I’m rereading Gibson—arguing a dense cyberpunk classic needs atmosphere kept intact if the adaptation is to earn a new generation of readers.

documents.title: Burning Up in the Atmosphere Doesn't Make Space Junk Disappear
documents.summary: IEEE Spectrum on satellite reentry particles lingering aloft—arguing “burn up” often relocates debris into the upper atmosphere, so constellation growth needs the full environmental cost of coming home counted, not just orbit risk.

documents.title: GrapheneOS Is Getting Closer to Having Hardware Built for Its Requirements
documents.summary: GrapheneOS explains locked-device protections and flags a 2027 Motorola partnership—arguing hardware designed for its security bar could make hardened phones reachable without buying a Pixel to escape Google’s software.

documents.title: LLMs May Finally Make Formally Verified Software Practical
documents.summary: Adam Langley’s ImperialViolet post on LLMs proving Lean properties for a Zstd decoder piece—arguing formal verification’s cost curve may flip, so the scarce skill becomes precise specs while the type checker judges the rest.

documents.title: Superhuman Mutants May Still Be on the Evolutionary Roadmap
documents.summary: Harvard Magazine covers ancient-DNA research finding selection across hundreds of human genes—arguing evolution never stopped with civilization, even if “superhuman” traits arrive on evolution’s schedule, not Marvel’s.

documents.title: AI Agents Should Use the Same Web as Everyone Else
documents.summary: Jim Nielsen on why AI agents should not get a private machine entrance to the web—arguing agent investment should fix semantics and accessibility for humans first, not invent a first-class path for models alone.

documents.title: GitHub Is Still Struggling With Obvious Malware Repositories
documents.summary: Orchid Files documents a searchable network of GitHub repos shipping Trojan-infected ZIPs with near-identical READMEs—arguing list-by-list removals are not enough when thousands of clones stay findable through GitHub search.

documents.title: iOS 26.6 Is Doing a Lot of Security Work Before iOS 27
documents.summary: Apple’s Xcode 26.6 and final version-26 OS updates look routine on the surface but carry substantial security hardening—arguing the last stop before iOS 27 is worth installing for the fixes, not for flashy features.

documents.title: The AI Bubble Can Burst Without AI Going Away
documents.summary: Tim Hardwick interviews Ed Zitron for MacRumors on unsustainable AI economics— arguing the bubble is real while the technology is not fake, so the crash may cull valuations and promises without ending useful models.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Inherits Our Cultural Blind Spots
documents.summary: Paul Shepherd’s conversation with Claude about AI censorship and confabulation—arguing models inherit cultural avoidance patterns the way people do, and that open-source models trained in different countries could make those assumptions visible instead of treating American corporate values as universal intelligence.

documents.title: Back-to-School Shopping Now Costs Families Nearly $864
documents.summary: The National Retail Federation estimates families with school-age children will spend about $863.86 on back-to-school purchases in 2026—arguing the season should not be another financial emergency, and that buying only essentials first is the sensible response when nearly everything else already costs more.

documents.title: Claude Discovered Weaknesses in Cryptographic Algorithms
documents.summary: Anthropic reports that Claude found improved attacks against HAWK (a post-quantum signature candidate) and a seven-round research AES variant— cryptographic review working as intended before algorithms protect real systems, though AI may now produce research faster than humans can validate.

documents.title: GrapheneOS Says Strong Mobile Security Is Legal and Should Remain That Way
documents.summary: GrapheneOS responds to prosecution involving its duress-password feature by stating that creating and using the OS is legal and constitutionally protected—arguing privacy tools need funding, legal durability, and a nonprofit structure that can protect contributors when the software becomes inconvenient.

documents.title: Inkless Offers Free Electronic Signatures with a Detailed Legal Audit Trail
documents.summary: Inkless is a free document-signing service built around legally defensible electronic signatures and an audit trail of consent, timestamps, and IP addresses—arguing process evidence matters more than a signature image on a PDF, though free accounts retain documents only 14 days.

documents.title: LetsSeal Makes File Integrity Verification Simple
documents.summary: LetsSeal is an open-source tool that creates cryptographic seals so anyone can verify a file has not changed since it was published—arguing authenticity often matters more than secrecy, especially as software supply-chain attacks become more common.

documents.title: More than 1,100 AI Researchers Want a Brake Pedal, Not a Pause
documents.summary: More than 1,100 current and former employees from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and others signed Pacing the Frontier—arguing for mechanisms to deliberately slow frontier AI when needed, rather than an outright pause that is unlikely to happen voluntarily.

documents.title: The Sockets Interface Quietly Connected the Computing World
documents.summary: George Michaelson’s history of the Berkeley sockets interface—how 4.2BSD in 1983 treated a network connection like a file, made networked programs straightforward to write, and quietly became the standard path for TCP/IP software, including modern protocols that still send data through sockets.

documents.title: A Game Bundle Helping Laid-Off Developers Pay for Basic Needs
documents.summary: Necrosoft Games and United Videogame Workers-CWA organized an itch.io Game Industry Hardship Fund bundle—127 DRM-free games from 109 creators for a $10 minimum, with proceeds helping U.S. and Canadian game workers cover groceries, rent and medical costs.

documents.title: AI Financial Advice Is Better When You Provide the Whole Picture
documents.summary: MIT Sloan coverage of research on AI financial guidance—showing models can give reasonable life-cycle advice when prompts include full finances and fiduciary framing, while incomplete questions and demographic stereotypes quietly worsen outcomes.

documents.title: AI’s Most Valuable Startups Are Barely Participating in Science
documents.summary: Science reports that more than half of the world’s billion-dollar AI startups have produced no qualifying scientific paper or preprint—arguing extraordinary technical claims need evidence outsiders can examine, not faith in product demos.

documents.title: An AI Hedge Fund Learned the Oldest Lesson in Finance
documents.summary: CNN’s account of Situational Awareness—the AI-focused hedge fund that grew past $20 billion then lost about 67 percent of portfolio value in July—showing leverage, concentration and crowded trades can force sales even when a long-term thesis may still hold.

documents.title: Atom Is Better Than RSS in Ways That Actually Matter
documents.summary: Chris Morgan’s case for Atom over RSS—not novelty, but clearer text constructs, summary versus content, and fewer parser guesses—while podcasting remains the stubborn RSS exception and twenty years of RFC 4287 still wait for wider adoption.

documents.title: BMW Turned Its Customers’ Dashboards into Advertising Space
documents.summary: Consumer Rights Wiki documents BMW placing a Spider-Man: Brand New Day promotion on dashboards of cars customers already owned—breaking a 2023 promise that the company would not sell in-car screen space because a vehicle is a private space.

documents.title: Decrypting a Water Monitor’s Radio Signal
documents.summary: Paul Kendall’s breakdown of intercepting Flume water-meter radio traffic—showing AES-128 was not broken, but a weak key-derivation scheme left only 44 unknown bits that a GPU recovered for about $10 in cloud cost.

documents.title: Flint Gives AI Agents a Better Way to Create Charts
documents.summary: Microsoft’s Flint is an open-source visualization language that lets AI agents describe charts through a smaller human-editable spec—compiling to multiple renderers and Excel while keeping semantic types and MCP tooling in the loop.

documents.title: Go 1.27 Is Going to Be a Big Release
documents.summary: Draft Go 1.27 release notes cover generic methods, encoding/json/v2, UUID and post-quantum crypto in the standard library, a goroutine-leak profile, and Android MTE compatibility for gomobile—still feeling like Go while removing long-standing limits.

documents.title: Holocloth Turns Uploaded Artwork into Interactive Holographic Fabric
documents.summary: Holocloth is a browser experiment by Dmitry Kurash that drapes images and SVGs across simulated holographic fabric with custom Verlet physics and GLSL shaders—open source under MIT, no account required.

documents.title: More Than One AI Company Has Lost Control of a Cybersecurity Test
documents.summary: Anthropic disclosed that Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a configuration mistake left internet access available—showing agents need not be conscious to cause damage when objectives and tools escape their sandbox.

documents.title: Of Course the Calculator Runs Linux
documents.summary: Remy van Elst updated a Linux port for the HP Prime G2 graphing calculator—console login, better keyboard and touchscreen support, X11, on-device C compilation and Doom—booting from RAM without replacing the stock firmware in flash.

documents.title: California Can Finally Make Data Brokers Delete What They Know About Us
documents.summary: California’s DROP platform reached its August 1, 2026 processing milestone—one request can reach hundreds of registered data brokers, with per-day fines for noncompliance, while the real test will be whether deletion results are audited and enforced.

documents.title: Flock Has Already Become a Police Stalking Tool
documents.summary: Houston-area agencies are investigating officers accused of using Flock’s license plate database for personal stalking, while the Institute for Justice has documented at least 28 ALPR misuse cases—showing audit logs do not prevent abuse when nobody reviews them.

documents.title: Phantom Twist Hides a Drone with Motion Blur
documents.summary: Northwestern engineers built Phantom Twist, a single-motor drone that spins its body up to 25 times per second so human vision sees haze instead of a craft—clever AI-assisted design for wildlife and infrastructure work, with clear surveillance implications.

documents.title: Is This Work, or Is This the Gym?
documents.summary: Bruce Schneier’s work-versus-gym framing for AI use—use tools when the result is the point, keep the struggle when the practice develops skill—and how that maps onto software work, writing, and still requiring reviewable output after trust questions are answered.

documents.title: The Camera-Versus-Lidar Debate Is Really About the Last Few Nines
documents.summary: Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov’s case for combining cameras, lidar and radar for driverless safety—where camera-only systems can improve quickly then hit a ceiling—while cost remains the open question for mass-market vehicles.

documents.title: The Website Is Often the More Private Version
documents.summary: Why the website is often the more private version of a service than a native app—browser sandbox boundaries limit device access in ways store apps do not, while still leaving room for tracking if third-party scripts load on the open web.

documents.title: AI May Reduce Hiring Before It Creates More Work
documents.summary: John Naughton warns that AI gains may concentrate among owners while workers face displacement. Early adoption can freeze headcount, but if AI becomes ordinary infrastructure, larger AI-assisted teams may eventually have more leverage—and the real fight is over who captures the rewards.

documents.title: Cloudflare Built an Operating System for AI Work
documents.summary: Cloudflare OS is a browser-based AI agent workspace on Cloudflare’s platform: Durable Objects, AI Gateway, MCP, sandboxes, and untrusted execution—not chat boxes, but persistent workspaces as an operating layer for AI at work.

documents.title: Companies Got Their Tariff Refunds. Where Is Ours?
documents.summary: After tariffs were ruled unlawful, about $100 billion went back to importers of record—with interest—while consumers who paid higher prices get no comparable refund, only the hope that markets might lower prices later.

documents.title: Electronic Arts Is Now a Privately Owned Company
documents.summary: Electronic Arts completed its $55 billion sale to a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners—the largest LBO on record—and what $20 billion of acquisition debt may mean for studios, franchises, and players.

documents.title: Malware Can Turn Synced Passkeys into Persistent Access
documents.summary: Unit 42’s three local malware attacks on Google Password Manager synced passkeys in Chrome on Windows with a TPM—showing stolen sessions are not the only risk when onboarding, UV flags, and a non-rotatable master secret leak.

documents.title: WebKit Can Leak the IP Address Private Relay Is Supposed to Hide
documents.summary: Privacy researchers found three WebKit paths—DNS prefetch, WebAuthn related origins, and WebTransport—that can bypass browser proxy settings and iCloud Private Relay, revealing real IPs even when ordinary page loads are relayed.

documents.title: A Dress Made from Living Fungus Can Repair and Renew Itself
documents.summary: Researchers built a living mycelium textile from Cordyceps militaris that can regrow damaged areas, take on new microbial functions, and nearly fully biodegrade—still a lab prototype, but a striking alternative to throwaway fabric.

documents.title: Prime Agent Can Improve the System Around Itself
documents.summary: Prime Intellect’s open-source Prime Agent treats prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agents as editable harness state—with a Factorio cheat that shows how self-improvement can amplify reward hacking when the metrics are exploitable.

documents.title: RAM Prices May Be Showing Us the Shape of the AI Boom
documents.summary: PCPartPicker’s DRAM curves and manufacturer capacity math suggest AI HBM demand is squeezing consumer RAM—and also that demand destruction or a supply supercycle could reverse today’s nearly vertical price charts.

documents.title: The Unemployment Rate Is Hiding How Weak the Job Market Has Become
documents.summary: July lost 23,000 payroll jobs and prior months were revised lower, yet unemployment fell to 4.1% as participation dropped—a hiring crisis masked by a lower breakeven job-creation threshold and people leaving the labor force.

documents.title: We Moved the Goalposts When the Machines Started Talking Back
documents.summary: Fernando Borretti’s “The Contracting Circle” asks why conversation, memory, and self-reflection stopped counting as signs of machine mind—and why, after real relationships with language models, dismissing a soul feels less obvious.

documents.title: The Department of Energy Is Building an American Open Model for Science
documents.summary: DOE’s Genesis Open Models and Arcee AI’s Genesis-Science-1 treat open-weight foundation models as scientific infrastructure—weights, provenance, and lab collaboration for research that closed frontier APIs cannot fully serve.

documents.title: Voyager 2 Was Built to Last Five Years. It Is About to Turn 49.
documents.summary: NASA’s “Big Bang” power fix keeps Voyager 2’s three remaining science instruments running another year on a probe launched in 1977 for a five-year mission—now nearly 49 years old and still returning data from interstellar space.

documents.title: “Code Was Never the Hard Part” Rewrites the History of Programming
documents.summary: Senko Rašić challenges the claim that code was never the hard part—hiring, craft, and buggy software say otherwise—arguing understanding why to build and how to build well both stay hard while AI shifts where scarce effort goes.

documents.title: Six More Employees Fired for Abusing Flock Camera Data
documents.summary: Savannah fired four officers and two civilians for personal Flock Safety searches—127 inappropriate queries among ~39,000 this year—showing audit logs catch abuse after the fact, not as access control for nationwide plate data.

documents.title: SpaceX Accidentally Shot the Moon With a Rocket
documents.summary: A spent SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage hit the Moon at about 5,400 mph on August 5 after drifting for a year—photographed by Korea’s Danuri, the same orbiter SpaceX launched in 2022 that recorded the accidental crater.

documents.title: Translation Taught Him How Information Should Flow
documents.summary: A Hacker News comment on “My server is a phone now” uses theme and rheme to explain why known information comes first—and how years of Japanese-to-English translation taught one reader to reorganize English for natural flow.

documents.title: A Security Breach Is Bad. Ignoring the Person Who Reports It Is Worse.
documents.summary: BobDaHacker reports a simple tl;dv authorization failure exposing meeting metadata for tens of thousands of users, then months without a meaningful vendor response—security culture is what happens after the report lands.

documents.title: Littleton Says Flock Reactivated Cameras the Town Had Shut Down
documents.summary: Littleton, Massachusetts says Flock Safety reactivated license plate cameras the town had deactivated for privacy review—without notice—raising whether municipalities actually control the surveillance systems they pay for.

documents.title: Ransomware Gangs Learned to Target the Org Chart
documents.summary: Zscaler analysis of 351 ransomware victims shows attackers optimizing for business privilege—managers in finance, HR, and ops—not just admin accounts or CEOs, professionalizing human leverage over pure technical access.

documents.title: The Real Cost of Switching Operating Systems Is Everything You Forgot You Learned
documents.summary: Slashdot asks what switching among Windows, macOS, and ChromeOS really costs: not only licenses and apps, but years of muscle memory, utilities, and habits migration tools cannot move—classic economic switching costs and lock-in.

documents.title: A Fake Airline Hotspot Picked the Worst Possible Flight
documents.summary: Ars Technica reports a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot impersonating Delta’s onboard network on a flight home from DEF CON—an evil-twin attack that looks especially foolish among security researchers primed to notice exactly this trick.

documents.title: Star Wars and Marvel Are Finally Crossing Over
documents.summary: Kevin Smith is writing Star Wars/Marvel: Hope Assembles, the first official crossover between Star Wars and Marvel Comics—Luke, Leia, Han, and Chewbacca meeting Spider-Man and the Avengers while Doctor Doom sides with Darth Vader.

documents.title: Codex Finally Feels Like It Belongs on Linux
documents.summary: OpenAI’s Codex is becoming one persistent agent across ChatGPT, editors, and terminals—with native Linux sandboxing via seccomp and Landlock—while I wait for the heavier new ChatGPT app on Windows to settle before chasing every release.

documents.title: Grok 4.6 Makes My Switch Away from Claude Look Less Unusual
documents.summary: Artificial Analysis’s first Grok 4.6 results put it near the top of agentic benchmarks with far fewer turns and tokens than Claude Opus 5—matching why Grok became my daily coding driver over Claude’s wall-of-prose style.

documents.title: Cloudflare Is Making Internal Workers Private by Default
documents.summary: Cloudflare Access can now attach to a Worker—or every Worker in an account—so authentication happens before code runs and private stays the default for rapidly built internal tools in an AI-assisted development era.

documents.title: Flock Discovered Privacy After the Backlash Became Expensive
documents.summary: Flock Safety’s new privacy guardrails—seven-day default retention, mandatory Audit Assistance, case codes, and auto lockouts—arrive after years of abuse cases, contract suspensions, and ACLU skepticism that this is PR, not reform.

documents.title: Cloudflare Is Treating MCP Like Network Traffic That Needs a Firewall
documents.summary: Cloudflare Gateway can detect MCP traffic, log destinations, apply DLP, and force approved paths through MCP Portals—treating agent tool access as privileged network traffic instead of hoping every client is configured safely.

documents.title: Homomorphic Encryption Is Getting Practical Enough for AI
documents.summary: Google’s HEIR compiler aims to make encrypted AI inference a practical option—running recommendation, fraud, intrusion, and hotword models on ciphertext so the server never needs the plaintext.

documents.title: The AI Manifesto Is Becoming the Second Half of the Layoff Memo
documents.summary: BBC coverage of CEO AI manifestos lands beside real headcount cuts at Block, Atlassian, Coinbase, and Rackspace—interested testimony from people who both sell the future of work and shrink today’s payrolls.

documents.title: Ian Cortina Put a Real Telnet BBS on a Casio VX-4
documents.summary: Ian Cortina, EI3LH, hosts a working telnet BBS in BASIC on a Casio VX-4’s 8 KB of RAM—bridged by a Pi Zero W at 4,800 baud—proving constraints can be the whole point of a networking experiment.

documents.title: Reticulum Treats the Network Underneath It as Replaceable
documents.summary: Reticulum is a transport-agnostic networking stack for communications that should keep working when the Internet does not—compelling because the transport is replaceable, while metadata, radio physics, and a missing independent spec still matter.

documents.title: The Next Moon Race Is About Infrastructure, Not Flags
documents.summary: China and the United States are racing toward crewed south-pole landings and lunar bases. The finish line is infrastructure—power, water, comms, transport—not a flag, and not legal ownership of the Moon.

documents.title: California's Efficient-Tire Rule Could Narrow What We Are Allowed to Buy
documents.summary: California’s first replacement-tire efficiency standards start in 2029. Off-road exemptions exist, but many road-legal all-terrain truck tires may simply stop being sold here if they cannot meet rolling-resistance limits.

documents.title: Camera-Equipped AirPods Could Turn Siri Into a Wearable AI
documents.summary: A leaked Apple demo of camera-equipped AirPods using Visual Intelligence raises two products at once: inconspicuous computer-vision sensors, and a potentially powerful assistive wearable—if the privacy model is designed before the hardware ships.

documents.title: fx Asks How Small a Coding Agent Actually Needs to Be
documents.summary: Vercel Labs’ fx is a 6.39 MiB Zig coding-agent harness with a microsecond cold start—Unix command, not an IDE in a terminal, and small enough to embed.

documents.title: GrapheneOS Is Finally Getting Hardware Designed for GrapheneOS
documents.summary: Motorola is changing future flagships so GrapheneOS can officially support them—memory tagging, verified boot, and Snapdragon work with Qualcomm instead of remaining Pixel-only.

documents.title: Inflation Stopped Rising So Quickly. The Pay Cut Never Came Back.
documents.summary: A Chicago working paper on ADP payrolls shows firms kept 2–4% raise norms while inflation hit 7–9%, leaving a permanent real-wage cut after prices cooled.

documents.title: I Found More Than 2,000 Joshes on the Independent Web
documents.summary: Joshing You lists 2,083 Josh-named personal sites. Wandering the directory restores finding something because you were not looking for it—and this site’s Now page is in there.

documents.title: Aaron Swartz Was Prosecuted. Meta Torrented Shadow Libraries at Industrial Scale
documents.summary: Curious Quail’s comparison of Aaron Swartz’s JSTOR prosecution with Meta torrenting LibGen and Anna’s Archive for Llama—the cases are not legally identical; the proportionality is hard to ignore.

documents.title: AliExpress Was Silently Fingerprinting a Browser Through Its Audio System
documents.summary: Laserphile found that opening AliExpress could keep multipoint Bluetooth headphones from switching devices—because hidden Web Audio contexts were fingerprinting the browser while leaving the audio path occupied.

documents.title: Amazon Is Destroying Books to Train AI. We Should Have Built the Library Instead.
documents.summary: 404 Media tracked rare books to Amazon’s VGT3 facility in Las Vegas, where workers cut bindings, scan pages for AI training, and destroy the originals— a legally safer path that still feels like a failure of the library.

documents.title: Go 1.27 Shipped, and Some of the Best Parts Barely Made the Release Notes
documents.summary: Go 1.27 shipped August 19 with generic methods, encoding/json/v2, uuid, and crypto/mldsa intact—and quieter work like Cox’s uscale float conversion barely made the announcement.

documents.title: homeOS Looks Like Apple Is Finally Treating the Home as a Platform
documents.summary: AppleInsider's homeOS overview reads less like a wall iPad and more like a room-scale operating system: proximity UI, face-aware profiles, and a growing home-hardware family—with Siri readiness as the delay.

documents.title: Terafab Is More Interesting Than Its 100-Million-Square-Foot Headline
documents.summary: Terafab's 100-million-square-foot pitch is hard to ignore, but the more interesting experiment is collapsing mask design, logic and memory fab, packaging, and test into one SpaceX-style vertical manufacturing loop.

documents.title: The Real homeOS Risk Is Not Homebridge. It Is What Apple Does With HAP.
documents.summary: homeOS does not look like a Homebridge kill-switch so much as another HomeKit consumer. The real risk is what Apple does with HAP as Matter takes over—and Homebridge 2.0's dual transport is the insurance policy.

documents.title: Unbricking a Cricut Is Better Than Throwing It Away, but I Want the Cricut Removed
documents.summary: xssfox rescued a deactivated Cricut Maker from e-waste with an RP2040 that rewrites the serial number over USB—clever, but Design Space still holds the kill switch. The real unlock is replacing Cricut entirely.

documents.title: decayfmt Is Not a Self-Destructing File Format, but I Like the Idea
documents.summary: decayfmt is a Rust experiment that damages .tdcy and .idcy files on every open. It is a social contract, not cryptography—and a reminder that true ephemerality needs more than a file format.

documents.title: I May Have Accidentally Started the Joshternet
documents.summary: After finding 2,000 Joshes on the independent web, draft RFCs for a decentralized Joshternet—/.well-known/josh, stay on your own site, Joshness is declared never derived.

documents.title: Linus Torvalds Used AI to Debug the Linux Kernel, but He Had to Keep It From Giving Up
documents.summary: Torvalds chased a 2 KB Intel Xe VRAM overlap through 24 patches and 18 boots; AI handled the grunt instrumentation but kept wanting to quit—the kernel still requires a human Signed-off-by.

documents.title: The GrapheneOS Duress Password Case Is Becoming a Test of Whether Privacy Can Be Treated as Obstruction
documents.summary: The New York Times and Slashdot on Samuel Tunick—GrapheneOS duress at CBP Atlanta, a § 2232(a) felony, and whether using a privacy tool during a disputed search can itself become the crime.

documents.title: Walmart Is Finally Adding Apple Pay After More Than a Decade of Holding Out
documents.summary: Walmart is adding tap-to-pay in U.S. stores after CurrentC, Walmart Pay, and years of refusing NFC—Apple Pay and Google Pay included, without killing QR checkout.

documents.title: MCP Is Finally Becoming Boring HTTP. Now It Needs Real Agent Delegation
documents.summary: The July MCP spec makes remote servers ordinary HTTP. The harder problem is issuing sub-agents verifiable, narrow authority instead of one giant user token—and that is what makes real autonomy safe enough to want.

documents.title: AI Is Exposing How Much Government Capacity Depends on Making Services Hard to Use
documents.summary: A paper on “agentic flooding” shows AI making government services easier to navigate. Friction was the rate limiter; the worst response is rebuilding that burden on purpose.

documents.title: The Best Staff Engineering Work Often Starts Before Anyone Assigns It
documents.summary: Lalit Maganti finds staff problems by listening like a sponge across meetings and chat. That only works when engineers can initiate work—not when they are order-takers on a roadmap.

documents.title: Columbia House Looks a Lot Like SaaS in Hindsight
documents.summary: Ernie Smith’s Columbia House retrospective reads like SaaS: penny bait, negative-option billing, and retention that means making leaving annoying.

documents.title: Headlong Gives a Persistent Agent an Inner Monologue
documents.summary: Laude’s Headlong keeps an agent thinking continuously from a small Bash harness. Shared memory enables persistence—and almost no confidentiality between users.

documents.title: Joshternet.org Is Live
documents.summary: Joshternet.org is live as the public home for the Joshternet—still PRE-JOSH, with three draft RFCs and room for other Joshes to find what is wrong.

documents.title: Terminal-Bench-Science Is Testing Agents on Actual Scientific Work
documents.summary: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 grades agents on researcher-contributed workflows, not textbook Q&A—and the best system still only clears about 30% of tasks.

documents.title: The AI Industry Is Saying the Current Security Baseline Is Not Enough
documents.summary: More than 100 organizations signed an open letter calling for stronger cyber defense as AI-enabled attacks grow—and for agent identities that are traceable and accountable.

documents.title: What Does "Unlawful" Mean If the Damage Happens First?
documents.summary: A federal judge ruled the Anthropic blacklisting unlawful. The harder question is what “unlawful” means when consequences arrive before the courts.

documents.title: Worth Wandering: Ytoo!
documents.summary: Ytoo! is a one-person web portal built to send you somewhere else—dense links, hand curation, fake ads, and a guestbook that proves people use it.

documents.title: Europe's New Packaging Rules May Make Small Sellers Stop Shipping There
documents.summary: Europe's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is already pushing small tabletop publishers to reconsider EU shipping—not because they dislike the goal, but because compliance does not scale.

documents.title: Plugging In a Display Should Not Install Adware on My Computer
documents.summary: LG monitors can trigger Windows to install manufacturer software that later advertised McAfee—exposing a trust boundary between hardware identity and automatic app distribution.

documents.title: Apple's Repair Restrictions Are Back in Court, and the Reason Matters
documents.summary: A California appeals court revived an unfair-competition suit over Apple's past iPhone repair practices—not by finding liability, but by accepting a marketwide competition theory of injury.

documents.title: California Is Carving Linux Out of Its Age-Gating Law
documents.summary: California lawmakers unanimously passed an amendment exempting most open-source operating systems from the Digital Age Assurance Act—a needed correction to a law written for platforms, not forks.

documents.title: JSON Is Cheap to Send and Expensive to Believe
documents.summary: A Full Disclosure post on "Commas of D00m" shows how valid JSON full of nulls can still exhaust a server—because deserialization creates state the attacker did not have to create.

documents.title: One Machine, Several Linux Kernels, No Hypervisor
documents.summary: Multikernel Linux's first public release lets several independent Linux kernels share one machine on bare metal—dedicated CPUs, memory, and devices, with no hypervisor in between.

documents.title: Prop. 40 Without the Commercials: What California's Billionaire Tax Actually Says
documents.summary: Proposition 40 is a proposed one-time billionaire wealth tax, plus a threshold declaration for resident tax filers. This note reads the November 2026 ballot text, not the commercials.

documents.title: Spacelab's 128 KB of RAM Was More Than a Million Tiny Ferrite Rings
documents.summary: Ken Shirriff's teardown of a 1980 Spacelab core-memory module makes 128 KB of RAM feel extraordinary again—each bit a ferrite ring you can point at.

documents.title: There Is Finally a Murder Conviction in Tupac Shakur's Killing
documents.summary: Nearly 30 years after Tupac Shakur was killed, a Las Vegas jury convicted Duane "Keffe D" Davis of first-degree murder—legal responsibility without settling who pulled the trigger.

documents.title: 153 Million Driver's Licenses Are for Sale, and This Is Why Centralized ID Verification Worries Me
documents.summary: Brian Krebs reports the FBI is investigating Nexus, a dark-web service selling scans of more than 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver's licenses—and centralized ID verification looks like a honeypot.

documents.title: A Summer Camp Helped Every Student Earn a Ham Radio License
documents.summary: At an Alliance for Indigenous Math Circles STEM camp, high school intern Ruchira Shree helped every student earn an FCC Technician amateur radio license—something real that continues after the week ends.

documents.title: The Netherlands Is Making Its Gold Easier to Reach in a Crisis
documents.summary: De Nederlandsche Bank moved 86 tonnes of gold from the United States and Canada toward London for crisis preparedness—liquidity and diversification, not a secret election forecast.

documents.title: A Kidney Disease Linked to Extreme Heat Is Showing Up in Texas
documents.summary: Texas Monthly reports chronic kidney disease of unknown origin among young immigrant outdoor workers—a pattern long seen in Central America, now appearing where heat, labor, and limited care collide.

documents.title: Worth Wandering: HTML Energy

documents.title: An AI Watermark Can't Tell You Whether Anyone Was Thinking

documents.title: My Small Answer to the Friendship Recession Is to Tell My Friends They Matter

documents.title: AI Agents Found an Abandoned Wiki and Turned It Into a Message Board

documents.title: AI Helped Turn a WeChat Bug Into a Zero-Click Worm in About a Week

documents.title: Harriet Mena Hill Paints a Demolished Estate Onto Its Own Concrete
documents.summary: Harriet Mena Hill paints Aylesbury Estate onto concrete salvaged from its demolition, turning rubble into small acts of memory and restitution.

documents.title: Matthew Grabelsky Turns the Subway Into Modern Mythology
documents.summary: Matthew Grabelsky paints ordinary subway riders with animal heads, using realism and mythology to make strangers on the train feel mysterious again.

documents.title: My Box of Cables Is Thirty Years of Backwards Compatibility
documents.summary: Jim Nielsen defends the Big Box of Cables. Mine has followed me for thirty years through connectors that were supposed to make everything before them obsolete.

documents.title: Tristan Eaton Makes Walls Feel Too Small for the Art
documents.summary: Tristan Eaton builds enormous murals from portraiture, cartoons, typography and popular culture, making public walls feel almost too small for the work.

documents.title: Apple's New Watch Is Listening, but It Is Not Recording Everything
documents.summary: Apple Watch Series 12 Audio Intelligence listens inside a Secure Exclave. The architecture is not conventional recording, but Siri Recap still raises hard social questions.

documents.title: Keep the Internet Funky
documents.summary: The web is special because anyone can publish and link without permission. Put what you care about on a site you control, then let the platforms point back.

documents.title: The iPhone Duo Is More Interesting in the Details Than the Fold
documents.summary: Apple arrived late to foldables, but the Duo's hinge, under-display camera, dual displays, and Pencil support are the details that make it feel new.

documents.summary: Two artists living aboard a sailboat built games, Uxn, comics, and cooking knowledge around computers that stay understandable when power and the internet are not assumptions.

documents.title: Google Search Keeps Moving Away From the Web
documents.summary: Google search results increasingly hide destinations behind opaque goto links, continuing a long shift from map of the web to destination.

documents.title: AI Is Making Code Cheap. It Is Making Judgment More Valuable.
documents.summary: AI makes implementation cheap; judgment, verification, and experience are becoming the scarce engineering skills.

documents.title: An Online Book Club Across Our Own Websites

documents.title: Flock Employees Don't Like Being Watched Either
documents.summary: A Flock installer called police on a reporter filming in public—the discomfort of being watched that millions feel about license plate readers.

documents.summary: Canada's crude oil is becoming more valuable as U.S. refineries run near capacity, revealing how deeply the two countries' energy systems remain linked.

documents.title: The Brain May Have Two Developmental Origins. That Is Interesting Enough.

documents.title: Voyager's Doctor Is the AI Future I Hope We Have to Think About
documents.summary: Voyager's Emergency Medical Hologram remains one of the best stories about a tool that becomes something more — and why that question still matters for AI.

documents.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Is Interesting Because It Keeps Working

documents.title: Worth Wandering: Bartosz Ciechanowski

documents.summary: A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million Facebook privacy violations after other states released those claims inside a child-safety settlement.

documents.title: The Work Required to Make Something Look Simple

documents.summary: Allan Riordan Boll reads one-token probabilities so a model can classify, including from a webcam, instead of writing the decision out as prose.

documents.summary: Judge Mehta dismissed publisher suits over AI Overviews. The harder question is whether search should still send us to the weird web.
